notes:
I found good material for most of verses 1–22. I couldn't use some sources because I ran out of searches and fetches before reaching them. The gaps are listed at the end.

**v. 1**
- **Audience and setting.** Guzik says Jesus did not climb the mountain to get away from the crowds. "Disciples" here means followers in a broad sense, not only the Twelve. Sitting was the normal posture for a teacher. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-5/
- **One sermon or a collection?** Ellicott thinks this is essentially the report of one real discourse, perhaps with a few additions from similar talks. He sees it as distinct from Luke's "Sermon on the Plain." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/5.htm
- **A different view on the same question.** Schaff's notes to Augustine list several opinions. He thinks it unlikely that Matthew and Luke report different sermons, because both begin with the same beatitude, and close with the same parable. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/schaff/npnf106.v.ii.i.html

**v. 2**
- **How Jesus spoke.** Guzik reads "opened His mouth" as Jesus speaking with energy and earnestness. He adds that the sermon does not present the political or material blessings of the Messiah's reign. Instead, it expresses the spiritual implications of the rule of Jesus in our lives. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-5/
- **Not a plan of salvation.** Guzik says the sermon is about how disciples live under Jesus as King, not about how one is saved. Ellicott warns against treating the sermon as the whole of Christian theology. He calls it the beginning of Jesus' teaching, "milk for babes." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/5.htm

**v. 3**
- **"Blessed."** Ellicott says the word describes a lasting state of happiness, not simply receiving a blessing from someone else. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/5.htm
- **Present tense.** Spurgeon, quoted by Guzik, notes that every blessing is in the present tense: "Blessed are," not "shall be." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-5/
- **Meaning of "poor in spirit."** Guzik says the word means the truly poor, who must beg for what they have. It is a confession that one is sinful and has nothing to offer God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-5/
- **Gill (Baptist, Calvinist).** The verse is not the poor in purse. It means people aware of their spiritual need who stand at "the door of mercy." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/5-3.html
- **Spurgeon on why this comes first.** He compares the beatitudes to a ladder whose first step must be near the ground, so that beginners can reach it. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/5-3.html
- **Spurgeon on what the beatitudes are for.** the object of our Saviour's discourse, which was to describe the saved, and not. to declare the plan, of salvation. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/5-3.html
- **Contrast with Luke 6:20.** Ellicott notes that Luke has only "poor," meaning outward poverty. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/5.htm

**Protestant vs Catholic on v. 3**
- **Matthew Henry** criticises those in the church of Rome, who vow poverty, and yet engross the wealth of the nations. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/5-3.html
- **An unnamed writer quoted on Precept Austin** calls self-mortification the whole error of monasticism. His point is that it only makes a person more aware of self. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew_53
- **Augustine (Catholic).** He reads the poor in spirit as those "not puffed up." He matches them to the fear of God, the first of the gifts of the Spirit listed in Isaiah. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/16011.htm

**v. 4**
- **Guzik.** The word for "mourn" is the strongest Greek word for grief. It means grief over sin, the "godly sorrow" of 2 Corinthians 7:10. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-5/
- **Ellicott.** The comfort promised includes pardon and peace. He links it to the "consolation of Israel" (Luke 2:25) and to the Holy Spirit as Comforter. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/5.htm

**v. 5**
- **Guzik.** Meekness is "strength under control," not weakness. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-5/
- **Ellicott.** He sees a possible allusion to Daniel 7:27. He also notes that many of the best manuscripts swap the order of verses 4 and 5. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/5.htm

**v. 6**
- **Ellicott.** He hears an echo of Jesus' own hunger in the wilderness. Desires for earthly goods end in frustration or boredom; only this hunger is promised to be filled. He compares John 4:14. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/5.htm

**v. 7**
- **Ellicott.** The idea is the same as in the Lord's Prayer, with James 2:13 as its negative side. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/5.htm
- **Guzik.** A merciful person choose[s] to think the best of them whenever possible and is compassionate toward outward sinners. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-5/
- **Augustine.** He says that they are blessed who relieve the miserable. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/16011.htm

**v. 8**
- **Ellicott.** "Heart" means desires and affections. The purity in view is not the Pharisees' outward, ceremonial kind. Nor is it only freedom from sexual sin; it also excludes hatred and greed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/5.htm
- **Augustine.** The pure in heart have a "pure eye" able to see eternal things. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/16011.htm

**v. 9**
- **Catholic Encyclopedia.** Peacemakers keep peace and restore it, both between people and between God and people. Quoting Gregory of Nyssa, it calls this "an imitating of God's love of man". https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/02371a.htm
- **Augustine.** He links peacemaking to wisdom, the seventh gift, and to being remade in God's image. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/16011.htm

**vv. 10–12**
- **Guzik.** The world persecutes these people because their values are the opposite of its own. He asks: if *no one* speaks evil of you, are these Beatitudes traits of your life? https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-5/
- **Spurgeon.** He counts seven beatitudes about character. The eighth is a blessing on those people when their excellence has provoked the hostility of the wicked. https://www.spurgeon.org/resource-library/sermons/the-beatitudes/
- **Augustine.** He counts seven stages leading to perfection, with the eighth showing what is perfect. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/16011.htm

**Catholic vs Protestant on vv. 3–12 as a whole**
- **Catholic.** Catholic Answers says the first seven beatitudes teach what actions, under the influence of the virtues and gifts of the Holy Spirit, merit an eternal reward. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/online-edition/the-greatest-beatitude
- **Aquinas on the rewards.** Interpreters disagree on whether the rewards are present or future. His answer: they are fully completed in the life to come but already begun in this life. https://www.newadvent.org/summa/2069.htm
- **Pope John Paul II (*Veritatis Splendor*).** The beatitudes are above all "promises," and a "self-portrait of Christ." https://www.newadvent.org/library/docs_jp02vs.htm
- **The Protestant side.** Compare Spurgeon's "describe the saved" (v. 3 above) and Guzik's view that the beatitudes are character traits the Spirit produces.

**vv. 13–16**
- **Salt and light.** Guzik says these are not roles we're called to become but realities of who we already are as disciples. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-5/
- **Not in isolation.** The figures show that beatitude character is to be lived out before the world, not apart from it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-5/
- **Parallel.** Ellicott pairs v. 13 with Luke 14:34. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/5.htm
- I found nothing more detailed on "losing savor" or "city on a hill."

**v. 17**
- **Guzik.** Jesus came to free it from the way the Pharisees and Scribes had wrongly interpreted it. He fulfilled both the predictions of the Law and its moral demands. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-5/
- **Calvin (Reformed).** He says Jesus here he treats of doctrine, not of life. Christ fulfilled the law by bringing "the dead letter" to life with his Spirit. Christ's coming took nothing away even from the ceremonies, but confirmed them by showing what they pictured. https://www.ccel.org/ccel/schaff/npnf106.v.ii.i.html is not the source here; see https://www.ccel.org/c/calvin/comment3/comm_vol31/htm/ix.xliii.htm
- **Matthew Henry.** The law is the Christian's rule of duty, and he delights therein. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/5-17.htm
- **Precept Austin.** Only the moral law still applies to believers; the ceremonial and civil laws were "fulfilled" in Christ. https://www.preceptaustin.org/matthew_517-20
- **Lutheran (1517.org).** The good news Jesus preached was the miracle of a fulfilled law, a completed righteousness, which was held out to the world on the basis of faith. https://www.1517.org/articles/the-gospel-of-a-fulfilled-law
- **Ligonier.** A Ligonier devotional on vv. 17–20 says Lutherans and Reformed agree on justification by faith. They differ in how they distinguish law and gospel. The snippet I saw did not explain the details. https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/law-and-gospel-2
- **Bible.org.** It notes that "fulfill" is read in about three main ways. https://bible.org/seriespage/not-abolish-fulfill
- **A second Bible.org writer.** He adds that Christ fulfills the law by giving believers power through the Spirit. https://bible.org/seriespage/11-proper-view-scripture-matthew-517-20

**v. 18**
- **Parallel.** Ellicott pairs this verse with Luke 16:17. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/matthew/5.htm
- **Perkins (Puritan).** He has a full exposition of vv. 17–20 on Monergism. I saw only its heading and summary. https://www.monergism.com/do-not-think-i-have-come-abolish-law-exposition-matt-517-20

**v. 19**
- **Matthew Henry.** Christ does not let his people trifle with any commands of God's holy law. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/5-17.htm

**v. 20**
- **Guzik.** He asks how anyone could exceed the Pharisees' devotion. His answer, drawing on v. 48, is that the law demands perfection. This shows we need the righteousness that comes by faith. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-5/
- **1517.org (Lutheran).** It reads v. 20 the same way: it points to the "completed righteousness" Christ offers through faith. https://www.1517.org/articles/the-gospel-of-a-fulfilled-law

**v. 21**
- **Guzik.** This is not "Jesus against Moses" but Jesus against false and superficial interpretations of Moses. The scribes reduced the command to the outward act alone. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-5/

**v. 22**
- **Guzik.** Jesus is *not* saying anger is as bad as murder. The law condemns both without making them the same thing. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/matthew-5/
- **Jamieson-Fausset-Brown.** Note the authoritative tone, as of the Lawgiver himself. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/5-22.htm
- **Gill.** "Fool" means a wicked reprobate man, not someone of low intelligence. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/5-22.htm
- **Another commentator on Bible Hub.** The three penalties stand for degrees of punishment in hell, not three earthly courts. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/5-22.htm
- **Chrysostom (Orthodox and Catholic Father).** As cited there, he took "Raca" as a contemptuous "thou." Others derive it from a word meaning "he spits." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/matthew/5-22.htm
- **A. B. Bruce.** "Raca" mocks a person's head ("you stupid!"). "Moros" ("fool") mocks their heart and character. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/60941/
- **Matthew Henry.** Insults are "tongue-murder." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/matthew/5-22.html
- **Textual note.** The KJV, NKJV and Majority Text add "without a cause." The BSB, NASB, ESV and Douay-Rheims leave it out. https://biblehub.com/matthew/5-22.htm

**vv. 23–24**
- None of the pages I read covered these two verses in detail. They need their own research.

**What I couldn't cover**
- **Wesleyan:** I did not reach wesley.nnu.edu or seedbed.com, so Wesley's sermons on this passage are missing.
- **Pentecostal and charismatic:** I found nothing from pneumareview, ag.org or samstorms. Enduring Word is the only source used from that group on your list.
- **Anglican:** I found no source.
- **Orthodox:** I have nothing from oca.org itself; Chrysostom appears only second-hand.
- **Modern scholarship:** I did not reach netbible.org or bibleodyssey.org.
- **Prosperity, word of faith and hyper-grace:** I found no material on how these teachings handle v. 3 or v. 5.
